learn: Health-related fitness has five parts: cardiorespiratory endurance, muscular strength, muscular endurance, flexibility and body composition.
Cardiorespiratory endurance is how well your heart and lungs supply oxygen during exercise.
Muscular strength is how much force a muscle can produce; muscular endurance is how long it can keep working.
check: Heart and lungs working together is...
How long a muscle can keep working is...
How many health-related components are there?
lessons.try: Do one activity for each component and record how it felt.

learn: Skill-related fitness includes agility, balance, coordination, power, reaction time and speed.
These help in sports: a goalkeeper needs reaction time; a gymnast needs balance.
Practice improves skill-related fitness.
lessons.try: Try a reaction-time ruler drop with a partner.

learn: Fitness tests measure your current level: a mile run, push-ups, sit-and-reach.
Compare yourself to your own past results, not to others.
Set SMART goals: Specific, Measurable, Achievable, Relevant and Time-bound.
check: The M in SMART stands for...
lessons.try: Write a SMART fitness goal for this month.

units.t: Warming Up, Cooling Down and the FITT Principle

learn: A warm-up raises heart rate and body temperature and prepares muscles.
Use dynamic stretches that move: leg swings, arm circles, walking lunges.
Warm up for 5 to 10 minutes before exercise.
lessons.try: Lead a five-minute dynamic warm-up.

learn: A cool-down lowers heart rate gradually after exercise.
Static stretches, held for 15-30 seconds, improve flexibility after exercise.
Never bounce in a static stretch.
check: In a static stretch you should not...
lessons.try: Do a five-minute cool-down with static stretches.

learn: FITT stands for Frequency, Intensity, Time and Type.
Frequency is how often; intensity is how hard; time is how long; type is which activity.
Adjust FITT to improve: gradually add time or intensity.
check: The I in FITT stands for...
lessons.try: Write a FITT plan for a week of cardio.

learn: Heart rate is the number of heartbeats per minute.
Find your pulse at your wrist or neck; count for 15 seconds and multiply by 4.
Resting heart rate for children is usually 70-100 beats per minute.
check: To find beats per minute from 15 seconds, multiply by...
A pulse can be found at the...
lessons.try: Measure your resting and post-exercise heart rate.

learn: Moderate activity raises your heart rate and breathing but lets you talk.
Vigorous activity makes it hard to say more than a few words.
Kids should get 60 minutes of moderate to vigorous activity daily.
check: Kids should be active ___ minutes daily.
lessons.try: Do the "talk test" during different activities.

learn: Aerobic activities like running, swimming and cycling build cardio fitness.
Interval training alternates hard and easy periods.
A stronger heart pumps more blood with each beat, so resting heart rate can drop.
check: A fitter heart pumps ___ blood per beat.
lessons.try: Try an interval workout: 30 seconds hard, 60 seconds easy, repeated six times.

learn: Invasion games (soccer, basketball, hockey) involve getting into the other team's area to score.
Offence means keeping possession and creating space; defence means closing space and blocking.
Moving to open space to receive a pass is key.
check: Moving to open space helps you...
lessons.try: Play a 3-on-3 passing game and count completed passes.

learn: Net games (volleyball, badminton, tennis) send an object over a net.
Aim for spaces the opponent can't reach.
Return to a ready position after each shot.
check: Aim for ___ the opponent can't reach.
lessons.try: Rally with a partner using a soft ball and a low net.

learn: Good teammates communicate, encourage and share the ball.
Sportsmanship means playing fairly, following rules and respecting opponents and officials.
Win with humility and lose with grace.
lessons.try: Give a teammate specific encouragement during a game.

learn: The six nutrients are carbohydrates, proteins, fats, vitamins, minerals and water.
Carbohydrates are the body's main energy source; protein builds and repairs muscles.
Healthy fats from nuts, fish and olive oil support the brain.
check: The body's main energy source is...
How many nutrient types are there?
lessons.try: List the nutrients in your lunch.

learn: MyPlate shows half your plate as fruits and vegetables.
The rest is grains (half of them whole grains) and protein, with dairy on the side.
Water is the best drink.
check: At least half your grains should be...
lessons.try: Design a healthy dinner plate.

learn: Nutrition labels show serving size, calories and nutrients.
Check for added sugars and sodium (salt), which should be limited.
Ingredients are listed from most to least.
check: The first thing to check is...
lessons.try: Compare the labels of two breakfast cereals.

learn: Children aged 6-12 need 9-12 hours of sleep each night.
Sleep helps memory, mood, growth and the immune system.
Screens before bed make it harder to fall asleep.
lessons.try: Keep a sleep diary for a week.

learn: Wash hands with soap for 20 seconds to stop germs.
Shower regularly and use deodorant as your body changes.
Brush teeth twice a day and floss daily.
lessons.try: Make a daily hygiene checklist.

learn: Puberty is when the body changes from a child's to an adult's, usually between ages 8 and 16.
Changes include growth spurts, more sweat, skin changes and changing feelings.
Everyone develops on their own timeline, and that's normal.
check: A common change in puberty is...
lessons.try: Write down a trusted adult you can ask about body changes.

learn: Emotions are signals: fear warns of danger; sadness shows loss; anger shows something feels unfair.
All emotions are normal; what matters is how we respond.
Naming an emotion helps you manage it.
lessons.try: Make a list of emotion words beyond happy, sad and mad.

learn: Stress is the body's response to a challenge, like a test or a big game.
A little stress can help focus; too much can harm health.
Healthy coping includes exercise, deep breathing, talking to someone and getting enough sleep.
lessons.try: Practise box breathing: breathe in 4, hold 4, out 4, hold 4.

learn: Talk to a trusted adult if feelings last a long time or feel too big.
School counsellors, parents and doctors can help.
Asking for help is a sign of strength.
check: Asking for help is a sign of...
Who can help with big feelings?
If feelings last a long time, you should...
lessons.try: List three trusted adults you could talk to.

learn: Healthy friends are kind, honest, supportive and respectful.
Friends can disagree and still respect each other.
Unhealthy friendships involve pressure, put-downs or controlling behaviour.
check: Constant put-downs are a sign of...
lessons.try: Write the top five qualities you want in a friend.

learn: Use "I" statements: "I feel upset when..."
Listen actively: make eye contact, nod and don't interrupt.
Body language and tone matter as much as words.
lessons.try: Role-play a disagreement using "I" statements.

learn: Peer pressure can be positive (studying together) or negative (doing something unsafe).
Refusal skills: say no firmly, give a reason, suggest something else, walk away.
If you see bullying, tell an adult and support the person being targeted.
check: If you see bullying, you should...
lessons.try: Practise saying no to a pressure situation.

learn: Wear the right protective gear: helmets, mouthguards and shin guards.
Stay hydrated by drinking water before, during and after exercise.
Stop if you feel pain and tell a coach.
check: If you feel pain, you should...
lessons.try: Make a safety checklist for your favourite sport.

learn: For minor cuts: wash, apply pressure to stop bleeding and cover with a bandage.
For sprains, remember RICE: Rest, Ice, Compression, Elevation.
In an emergency, call for help: 911 in the United States.
check: RICE stands for Rest, Ice, Compression and...
lessons.try: Practise wrapping a pretend sprained ankle.

learn: Never share passwords, your address or your school online.
Strangers online may not be who they say they are.
Tell a trusted adult if anything online makes you uncomfortable.
lessons.try: Check the privacy settings of an app with a parent.

learn: Lifetime activities can be enjoyed at any age: walking, swimming, cycling, hiking, yoga, dance.
Choosing activities you enjoy makes it easier to stay active.
Active adults have lower risk of heart disease and better mood.
check: Staying active is easier when you...
lessons.try: Try a new lifetime activity this week.

learn: Yoga combines poses, breathing and focus.
Poses like tree, warrior and child's pose build balance, strength and calm.
Move slowly and never force a stretch.
lessons.try: Hold tree pose for 30 seconds on each foot.

learn: Hiking, orienteering and cycling build fitness outdoors.
Plan routes, check weather and tell someone where you're going.
Leave No Trace: take your rubbish home and respect wildlife.
lessons.try: Plan a family walk with a map.
